src/user/user.controller.ts login(): `if (!_user) throw new HttpException({errors}, 401);` turns a missing result into an HTTP status, which is a presentation concern

src/user/user.controller.ts login(): credential checking (findOne) and token creation (generateJWT) are handed to the application-layer UserService; the controller only orders the two calls, which is borderline orchestration but not a business rule
parsedVerdict.reasoning: UserController is in the presentation layer. Its jobs fit that role: it routes HTTP requests with NestJS decorators, binds request bodies and params, attaches validation pipes and Swagger metadata, and hands work to UserService. findMe, update, create and delete just pass calls through to the service. login is the only method with real logic. It calls userService.findOne, turns a missing user into an HTTP 401 with HttpException, gets a token from userService.generateJWT, and builds the response object. Turning a missing result into an HTTP status and shaping the response are presentation work. Choosing to fetch the user first and then create a token is light use-case orchestration that could sit in the application layer. But the actual rules (checking credentials, signing the JWT) stay in the service. The controller holds no persistence, domain rules or infrastructure code. This is a minor smell, not a clear rubric failure.
